header:
Date: 2025-02-18T15:00:00Z
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE); Arjun Patel (Redwood SE); Lisa Chen (CTO, Acme); Tom Ruiz (ML Eng, Acme); Priya Singh (Infra Lead, Acme)
summary: Deep dive into repeated OOMs and intermittent CUDA allocation failures observed by Acme when running a 13B model in their VPC on-prem environment. Discussed root causes: batch-induced KV cache growth, driver/CUDA mismatches, NCCL hangs causing timeouts, and retry semantics that amplify thundering herds. Agreed next steps to collect kernel and GPU logs, run reduced-batch repros, and test a prewarmed dedicated instance with conservative batch limits and adjusted retry/backoff policies.
transcript: [00:00:00] Sofia Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? we got about an hour.
[00:00:08] Lisa Chen: Lisa here, CTO. we've got production jobs hitting OOMs and sometimes the pods go into crashloop backoff, so hoping to figure out why.
[00:00:18] Arjun Patel: Thanks Lisa. Tom, Priya — could you describe the infra? are you on-prem racks or cloud VPC?

[00:00:25] Priya Singh: We're a hybrid, most of inference is in our VPC with on-prem GPU hosts (A100 80GB), running k8s 1.25, nvidia driver 525, CUDA 11.7 in containers. using the nvidia-container-toolkit.
[00:00:38] Tom Ruiz: We see the OOMs typically at high concurrency, occasional CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED, and then timeouts at the gateway. Sometimes the process logs a CUDA error 2 then dies.

[00:00:50] Arjun Patel: Ok that matches a few common patterns. two axes: real GPU memory exhaustion from KV cache/batching, and secondarily driver/runtime mismatches triggering allocation failures. been seen both.
[00:00:58] Lisa Chen: Quick question, we run quantized 8-bit models for cost reasons. could that interact?

[00:01:04] Arjun Patel: Yes — quantization reduces activation/model mem but can increase temporary workspace or change allocator behavior; also 4-bit/8-bit implementations sometimes rely on different kernels with different cublas/cuBLAS workspace needs. so you can still hit OOMs.
[00:01:20] Sofia Martinez: Let's get concrete: what's your typical request shape and batch size?

[00:01:25] Tom Ruiz: Average sequence length ~512 tokens; we use dynamic batching with max_batch_tokens 4096; p99 latency target is 200ms. during spikes we see many small requests that get batched, so effective batch sometimes jumps to ~8 concurrent small requests.

[00:01:40] Arjun Patel: That max_batch_tokens 4096 with seq 512 implies batch_size ~8, that squares with Tom's observation. KV cache for chat-style workloads also grows with context; if clients send long histories the KV can blow past expected footprint.
[00:01:53] Priya Singh: We also observed that failure correlates with cold-starts after node reboots.
[00:01:58] Arjun Patel: Cold starts can cause memory fragmentation. driver versions and CUDA ABI mismatch can make alloc fail early. can you confirm exact driver vs CUDA inside container?
[00:02:08] Priya Singh: We'll provide nvidia-smi output; currently driver 525.85 and container image built with CUDA 11.7.
[00:02:15] Arjun Patel: That should usually be ok, but small ABI diffs matter. also check nvidia-persistenced, and that no other processes are using GPU memory (monitor via nvidia-smi -q).
[00:02:25] Tom Ruiz: We did see kernel OOM messages around the time of failures in dmesg once. not frequent but present. could cgroups be letting the kernel kill processes?

[00:02:34] Arjun Patel: Kernel OOM suggests host-level memory pressure — if GPU pinned memory or CPU OOM happens, kernel may OOM the process. also kubelet eviction thresholds if node memory is constrained.
[00:02:44] Lisa Chen: What about retry semantics: when the gateway times out we have client retries, could that be making things worse?

[00:02:49] Arjun Patel: Absolutely — retry storms are classic. if request times out at proxy and clients immediately retry with no jitter, you multiply concurrency. We recommend idempotent request tracking and exponential backoff with jitter. also server-side queue limits and backpressure (429) instead of letting load pile up.
[00:03:05] Sofia Martinez: We shipped a doc on retry/backpressure patterns, I'll share the link after the call. It includes sample client code to implement exponential backoff and circuit breaking.
[00:03:12] Tom Ruiz: When the error is CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED we see calls stacktrace pointing to cuBLAS alloc during matmul initialization. Any mitigation?

[00:03:19] Arjun Patel: Mitigations: 1) reduce max_batch_tokens or enforce smaller per-request token limits, 2) enable per-worker prewarming so kernels/loaders allocate early while node is idle, 3) consider limiting number of concurrent model worker replicas per GPU, 4) for quantized models try 8-bit kernels known to be memory-friendlier or enable mixed CPU/GPU kv cache.
[00:03:36] Priya Singh: Mixed CPU/GPU kv cache? how does that affect latency?

[00:03:40] Arjun Patel: There's a trade-off — keeping KV on CPU reduces GPU resident memory but increases latency for cache hits due to PCIe transfer. Redwood supports a mode to offload older KV blocks to host, configurable by age/size thresholds. For p99-sensitive paths we keep small hot KV on GPU and spill cold KV to CPU.
[00:03:57] Lisa Chen: the timeouts we see sometimes are NCCL hangs, how do we debug that?

[00:04:02] Arjun Patel: NCCL hangs often present as long stalls rather than immediate OOM. collect CUDA stack traces (cuda-gdb or jstack of process) and check for NCCL version mismatches. Also check network fabric (RDMA) and driver/kernel logs because NCCL uses IB for multi-GPU and that can deadlock if drivers mismatch. In single-GPU cases, NCCL shouldn't be in the critical path unless using multi-instance or PCI switching.
[00:04:21] Tom Ruiz: We have single GPU per pod but we do use MIG sometimes. could MIG cause allocation failures?

[00:04:26] Arjun Patel: MIG slices change available memory and can cause surprising limits; confirm the MIG config. also some container runtimes don't report MIG correctly and the scheduler might overcommit.

[00:04:34] Sofia Martinez: A few pragmatic checks: provide kernel and dmesg, container inspect, image CUDA version, exact model size and quant flags, and a sample request that reproduced the error. We'll correlate with our server logs.
[00:04:44] Priya Singh: We'll collect nvidia-smi -q, dmesg, pod yaml and perf top if needed.

[00:04:49] Arjun Patel: On Redwood side we'll look at allocator logs: when we see CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED we log the attempted alloc size; share the debug artifacts and we'll map alloc patterns to KV/batch growth. Also try the repro with these knobs: max_batch_tokens=2048, max_concurrent_requests=4, prewarm=on.
[00:05:05] Tom Ruiz: Are there environment variables or driver flags that help with fragmentation?

[00:05:09] Arjun Patel: A few: set CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES properly, use CUDA_MALLOC_ASYNC if available, and try limiting GPU memory growth in the runtime (our runtime supports an env for reserve and growth). Additionally, enabling unified memory fallback as last resort can avoid hard OOMs at a cost in latency.
[00:05:25] Lisa Chen: We're also on a VPC private deployment. any difference compared to Redwood hosted?

[00:05:30] Arjun Patel: In private deployments you manage drivers and host-level settings; on Redwood hosted we manage image-driver pairing and pre-test kernels. So common causes on private are driver mismatches, different kernel modules, or security restrictions (seccomp) preventing device access. We can share our driver/OS matrix.
[00:05:44] Tom Ruiz: A quick note — we saw 'CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY' then immediate crash, but sometimes the process is killed by the kernel OOM. Which is earlier?

[00:05:51] Arjun Patel: If GPU allocation fails, runtime will error first; kernel OOM is usually due to pinned memory or host memory pressure. look at timestamps in dmesg vs container logs. often it's a combination: memory spike on host triggers kernel OOM which takes out the process while GPU had remaining allocations. it's messy.
[00:06:06] Priya Singh: On timeouts, do you recommend server-side 429 vs 504?

[00:06:10] Arjun Patel: Prefer 429 with Retry-After when you have queueing limits; use controlled rejection to avoid thundering herd. 504 with immediate retry from client will amplify load. Also implement circuit-breakers that mark a model replica unhealthy if it's repeatedly hitting OOM.

[00:06:22] Sofia Martinez: We also talked about retry idempotency — for chat completions it's tricky because partial tokens may be emitted. Redwood supports at-most-once delivery with request ids and token-offset reconciliation. We'll include that in the doc.
[00:06:32] Tom Ruiz: About quantization: we are using a 4-bit experimental build in some branches — should we avoid that in prod?

[00:06:38] Arjun Patel: 4-bit is great for costs but kernels are newer and less mature; they can have different workspace requirements and sometimes rely on swapped-in CPU kernels for certain ops. For stability prefer 8-bit in prod unless you can validate with sustained load.
[00:06:48] Lisa Chen: Any quick wins we can try before next week?

[00:06:51] Arjun Patel: Yes: 1) reduce max_batch_tokens to 2048, 2) cap concurrent requests per worker to 4, 3) enable prewarming and reserve ~10% GPU headroom, 4) enable exponential backoff + jitter on clients, 5) run repro with identical docker image and collect logs.
[00:07:03] Priya Singh: We'll try those and send logs. Also, if driver mismatch is root cause, what's the recommended driver/CUDA pairing?

[00:07:10] Arjun Patel: We'll share our driver/CUDA matrix; generally latest driver for your kernel plus CUDA 11.7 is fine for A100 but confirm minor versions. We'll attach exact combinations that we validated.
[00:07:18] Sofia Martinez: I'll share a short checklist and our internal playbook on OOM triage. Also attaching a link to a benchmark sheet and the retry patterns doc.
[00:07:25] Lisa Chen: Great. One last thing — if we want Redwood Dedicated seats to try a canary run, what's typical lead time?
[00:07:31] Sofia Martinez: We can spin up a small dedicated pool for a pilot in 3-5 business days after order; we'll do a prewarm and run the same workload. We'll follow up with pricing and SOW.
[00:07:40] Tom Ruiz: Thanks all. we'll get logs in the ticket.
[00:07:44] Arjun Patel: Thanks, we'll analyze and revert.
[00:07:46] Sofia Martinez: OK recap: Redwood to send triage checklist and driver matrix; Acme to send logs and run reduced-batch repro; follow-up canary week of 2025-02-24. Meeting end.
[00:07:55] --- End of transcript (approx) ---
